title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 6
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: The Formation of Coral Reefs
passages.text:
Coral reefs are among Earth's most productive ecosystems, harboring roughly one-quarter of all marine species despite occupying less than 0.1 percent of the ocean floor. These underwater structures, built by tiny colonial animals called corals working in concert with symbiotic algae, represent some of the largest biological structures on the planet, visible even from space. Yet the process by which these spectacular ecosystems form remains a topic of ongoing scientific investigation, as researchers work to understand the ecological conditions that allow corals to thrive and the mechanisms by which they construct their massive stone skeletons.

At the foundation of coral reef formation lies a fundamental biological partnership: the symbiosis between coral polyps and zooxanthellae, single-celled dinoflagellate algae living within coral tissues. The coral polyp provides the zooxanthellae with a protected environment and access to inorganic compounds derived from the coral's metabolism. In return, the zooxanthellae photosynthesize, converting sunlight into energy-rich organic compounds that nourish the coral host. This relationship is so intimate that neither organism can survive long in healthy condition without the other in tropical reef environments. The zooxanthellae photosynthesis is crucial; in fact, it explains why coral reefs are restricted to shallow, clear tropical waters where light penetrates sufficiently for algae to function—reefs rarely form deeper than 50 meters or in cold water, regardless of other favorable conditions.

Coral polyps construct their calcium carbonate skeletons through a process called calcification. As the polyp extracts calcium ions and dissolved inorganic carbon from surrounding seawater, it combines these ions within specialized cellular compartments to form calcium carbonate crystals, gradually building the rigid structure that gives the reef its architecture. Different coral species precipitate calcium carbonate in characteristic structural patterns: some build branching formations resembling antlers, others form massive hemispherical structures, and still others create delicate plate-like formations. This architectural diversity serves important ecological functions—branching corals create habitat complexity and shelter for smaller reef organisms, while massive corals provide stable substrate for encrusting organisms and endure higher wave stress in exposed reef zones.

The process of reef growth is remarkably slow, with most reef-building corals adding only 5 to 40 millimeters of skeletal material per year. Yet in favorable conditions—warm water between 25 and 29 degrees Celsius, adequate light, moderate water movement, and sufficient nutrient availability—reefs can accumulate to substantial thicknesses. Over millennia, successive generations of corals have built some reefs to depths exceeding 1,000 meters, as documented in the Great Barrier Reef and other major reef systems. The longevity of individual coral colonies compounds this slow accumulation: some coral species can survive for centuries or even millennia, with the oldest known coral specimens exceeding 4,000 years of age.

Contemporary coral reefs face unprecedented stressors that threaten their survival. Warming ocean temperatures trigger coral bleaching, a catastrophic process in which corals expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae in response to thermal stress, causing the coral to lose its pigmentation and its primary energy source. Since the 1980s, coral bleaching events have increased dramatically in frequency and severity, with the 2016 global bleaching event affecting roughly 30 percent of the world's coral reefs. Ocean acidification—the dissolution of atmospheric carbon dioxide into seawater, lowering pH—makes calcification energetically more costly for corals and can dissolve existing skeletons. Pollution, overfishing, and destructive fishing practices add further stress. Despite comprising less than 1 percent of the ocean's surface area, coral reefs generate approximately 375 billion dollars annually in ecosystem services including fisheries support, tourism, and coastal protection, making their conservation economically critical alongside its ecological necessity.

passages.title: Renewable Energy: Solar Power Technology
passages.text:
Solar power technology, which converts sunlight directly into usable energy through photovoltaic cells or solar thermal collectors, has emerged as one of the fastest-growing renewable energy sectors globally. The fundamental advantage underlying solar energy's expansion is conceptually straightforward: the sun delivers more energy to Earth's surface in one hour than all humans consume in an entire year. Yet translating this abundant resource into reliable, economical electricity has required sustained technological innovation, and ongoing advances continue to improve efficiency, reduce manufacturing costs, and expand potential applications.

Photovoltaic technology, which directly converts photons into electrical current through the photovoltaic effect, represents the most widely deployed solar technology. When light strikes a semiconductor material such as silicon, photons excite electrons to higher energy states, creating electron-hole pairs. If these charge carriers are separated by an electric field created by a junction of positively-doped and negatively-doped semiconductor material—the fundamental structure of a p-n junction—the separation generates electrical current that can be collected through metal contacts and delivered to external circuits. The efficiency of this conversion process has improved dramatically over recent decades. First-generation crystalline silicon panels, commercially available since the 1950s, achieved roughly 6 percent efficiency; contemporary high-efficiency monocrystalline silicon panels exceed 22 percent efficiency in commercial production, with laboratory prototypes achieving over 40 percent efficiency through multi-junction designs using different semiconductor materials.

In addition to silicon-based photovoltaics, emerging technologies promise further efficiency gains and cost reductions. Perovskite solar cells, manufactured from halide perovskite materials, have demonstrated laboratory efficiencies exceeding 30 percent in recent years and offer several advantages: they can be manufactured at lower temperatures using simpler chemical processes than silicon cells, potentially reducing production costs significantly. Thin-film photovoltaics, which deposit semiconductor material in extremely thin layers on glass or plastic substrates, consume less raw material than conventional silicon cells and exhibit superior performance in low-light or diffuse-light conditions common in cloudy climates. Organic photovoltaics, based on carbon-based polymers, offer the promise of flexible, lightweight, potentially transparent solar cells suitable for integration into building materials and other applications impossible with rigid crystalline silicon panels.

Beyond photovoltaic technologies, concentrated solar power (CSP) systems employ mirrors or lenses to concentrate sunlight, heating fluids to extremely high temperatures that drive conventional turbines to generate electricity. CSP systems can incorporate thermal storage, allowing facilities to generate electricity even after sunset by releasing stored heat, addressing a critical limitation of basic photovoltaic systems: intermittency and mismatch between peak solar generation during daytime and peak electricity consumption during evening hours. Some CSP facilities achieve capacity factors exceeding 50 percent through thermal storage, whereas conventional photovoltaic installations typically achieve capacity factors of 15 to 25 percent.

The fundamental challenge confronting solar expansion remains grid integration and energy storage. While solar capacity has grown exponentially—global installed photovoltaic capacity exceeded 1 trillion watts (1 terawatt) in 2023—this represents only approximately 4 percent of global electricity generation. The intermittency inherent in solar generation, where cloud cover and seasonal variations create fluctuating output, requires either energy storage systems (batteries or thermal storage) or grid flexibility to absorb variable supply. Battery storage technologies, particularly lithium-ion batteries, have experienced dramatic cost reductions of over 90 percent in the past decade, making solar-plus-storage systems increasingly economically competitive with fossil fuel generation. Continued deployment and technological advance in both solar generation and energy storage technologies will be essential for solar power to achieve its potential as a primary global energy source.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what percentage of marine species are found in coral reefs despite their limited area?
questions.correctAnswer: Roughly one-quarter
questions.explanation: The passage states coral reefs harbor 'roughly one-quarter of all marine species despite occupying less than 0.1 percent of the ocean floor.'
options: Roughly one-quarter
Roughly one-half
Roughly three-quarters
Roughly one-tenth

questions.prompt: The word 'symbiosis' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: a mutually beneficial relationship between organisms
questions.explanation: Symbiosis refers to a close relationship where both organisms benefit; the passage describes how corals and zooxanthellae depend on each other.
options: competition between organisms
a mutually beneficial relationship between organisms
parasitic relationship where one harms another
random association of unrelated species

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the maximum depth at which coral reefs typically form?
questions.correctAnswer: Deeper than 50 meters is rarely observed
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states 'reefs rarely form deeper than 50 meters' due to insufficient light for zooxanthellae photosynthesis.
options: Depth has no effect on reef formation
Deeper than 200 meters in most cases
Deeper than 50 meters is rarely observed
Deeper than 1,000 meters in favorable conditions

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from the passage about why zooxanthellae are essential to reef formation?
questions.correctAnswer: Zooxanthellae provide the energy necessary for coral growth through photosynthesis
questions.explanation: The passage explains zooxanthellae photosynthesize to provide 'energy-rich organic compounds that nourish the coral host,' and coral reefs require sufficient light for this process.
options: Zooxanthellae protect corals from physical damage
Zooxanthellae attract fish to coral reefs
Zooxanthellae construct the calcium carbonate skeletons
Zooxanthellae provide the energy necessary for coral growth through photosynthesis

questions.prompt: Why does the author discuss the different structural patterns of coral species in paragraph 3?
questions.correctAnswer: To explain how architectural diversity serves different ecological functions
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes various coral structures and then explains how each type serves specific ecological purposes for the reef ecosystem.
options: To explain how architectural diversity serves different ecological functions
To argue that humans should collect different coral species
To prove that coral skeletons are not made of calcium carbonate
To show that all corals are identical in structure

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a requirement for healthy reef growth?
questions.correctAnswer: Absence of all fish species
questions.explanation: The passage mentions warm water temperatures, light, water movement, and nutrient availability, but not the absence of fish.
options: Moderate water movement
Absence of all fish species
Warm water between 25 and 29 degrees Celsius
Adequate light penetration

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the range of annual skeletal growth for most reef-building corals?
questions.correctAnswer: 5 to 40 millimeters per year
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states 'most reef-building corals adding only 5 to 40 millimeters of skeletal material per year.'
options: More than 200 millimeters per year
1 to 5 millimeters per year
5 to 40 millimeters per year
50 to 100 millimeters per year

questions.prompt: The word 'expel' in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: force out or discharge
questions.explanation: Expel means to force something out; corals 'expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae' during bleaching events.
options: protect or shelter
synthesize or produce
absorb or incorporate
force out or discharge

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential meaning of: 'Ocean acidification—the dissolution of atmospheric carbon dioxide into seawater, lowering pH—makes calcification energetically more costly for corals and can dissolve existing skeletons.'
questions.correctAnswer: Ocean acidification harms corals by making calcium carbonate production more difficult
questions.explanation: The sentence describes how lower pH increases the energy cost of calcification and threatens existing structures.
options: Ocean acidification harms corals by making calcium carbonate production more difficult
Atmospheric carbon dioxide has no effect on oceans
Coral skeletons become harder when pH increases
Carbon dioxide improves coral growth

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.correctAnswer: A,B,D
questions.explanation: These capture the main themes: the symbiotic foundation of reefs (A), the slow building process through calcification (B), and contemporary threats (D).
options: A. Coral reefs depend on symbiosis between corals and zooxanthellae, which limits reefs to shallow tropical waters.
B. Corals slowly build their calcium carbonate skeletons in characteristic patterns that serve different ecological functions.
C. Coral reefs are not productive ecosystems compared to terrestrial forests.
D. Contemporary stressors including warming, acidification, and pollution threaten coral reef survival globally.
E. Coral bleaching was first discovered in the year 2016.
F. Coral reefs provide no economic benefits to human societies.

options: More energy in one day than humans consume in one year

Roughly equal to current human consumption

About 30 percent
About 50 percent
More than 90 percent

questions.prompt: The word 'intermittency' in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: inconsistent or irregular output
questions.explanation: Intermittency refers to the irregular or inconsistent nature of solar generation due to weather and time of day.
options: inconsistent or irregular output
expensive and inefficient
rapid and sudden changes
constant and reliable

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential meaning of: 'The intermittency inherent in solar generation, where cloud cover and seasonal variations create fluctuating output, requires either energy storage systems or grid flexibility to absorb variable supply.'
questions.correctAnswer: Solar power's variable output needs storage systems or flexible grids to work reliably
questions.explanation: The sentence explains how the inconsistent nature of solar generation requires technological or infrastructure solutions.
options: Energy storage systems are completely unnecessary for solar power
Solar power's variable output needs storage systems or flexible grids to work reliably
Grid flexibility cannot accommodate solar power generation
Solar power always generates maximum electricity regardless of conditions

questions.prompt: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.correctAnswer: A,C,E
questions.explanation: These capture the main themes: solar's enormous potential (A), advancing photovoltaic efficiency and emerging technologies (C), and challenges requiring energy storage solutions (E).
options: A. The sun delivers vastly more energy to Earth than humans currently consume, making solar power potentially scalable.
B. First-generation silicon panels were more efficient than contemporary panels.
C. Photovoltaic efficiency has improved dramatically, and emerging technologies like perovskite and thin-film cells offer further advances.
D. Concentrated solar power systems are inferior to photovoltaic systems in every way.
E. Solar expansion requires solving the intermittency challenge through energy storage and grid integration technologies.
F. Solar power currently provides more than half of global electricity generation.
